# The Misconception of Idle Charging and Alternator Limits

Running an engine in neutral solely to recharge a deeply discharged battery is fundamentally inefficient, regardless of whether you hold it at 1,000 RPM or idle at 600 RPM. While the alternator generates electricity whenever the engine spins, the vehicle's own electrical consumption creates a ceiling that prevents effective charging while stationary. In an automatic transmission car with failing brakes, this method will likely result in a net energy loss rather than a gain.

To understand why, we must look at the balance sheet of the alternator system. The alternator is driven by the serpentine belt connected to the crankshaft. Its output voltage and current are directly proportional to engine speed (RPM), but only up to a saturation point where the internal diode resistance limits further gain. More critically, every component on the electrical grid draws power simultaneously: ignition coils, fuel pumps, cooling fans, ECU processing, dashboard illumination, and most notably, the alternator's own self-excitation circuit.

If your battery is weak but can start the engine, it likely has a voltage below 12V or significantly reduced capacity. When you crank the starter motor, it draws hundreds of amps for a few seconds, draining whatever residual charge remains instantly. Once the engine starts, the alternator begins charging at idle (typically around 50–70 RPM in an automatic). However, most modern vehicles require approximately 800 to 1,200 RPM just to overcome internal friction and drive accessories like the water pump and power steering pump without straining the belt. At these "minimum operational" speeds, the alternator output often matches or slightly exceeds the parasitic drain of the vehicle systems when idling.

The critical flaw in this approach is that a battery cannot be charged if its terminal voltage is lower than the system's charging voltage threshold. A typical lead-acid battery needs roughly 13.8V to 14.2V across its terminals to accept a meaningful charge current. If your resting battery voltage is below 12.5V, simply running the engine at idle might not raise the alternator output high enough to push net current *into* the battery against the internal resistance of a deeply discharged cell. The system may reach equilibrium where generation equals consumption, leaving the battery sitting at 12.6V indefinitely without actually replenishing its chemical reserves.

Furthermore, duration is irrelevant if the physics of the situation dictate zero or negative charge flow. Running an engine for four hours in neutral does not magically inject more energy than it consumes through friction and parasitic loads. In fact, prolonged idling can be detrimental to the battery itself. A lead-acid battery held at a low state of charge for extended periods suffers from sulfation, where lead sulfate crystals form on the plates, permanently reducing capacity. This process is irreversible once the crystals grow too large.

If you cannot drive the vehicle due to brake issues, the mechanical solution involves decoupling the alternator's output from the vehicle's drain. You would need a DC-DC charger or an external power source capable of forcing current into the battery at 14V+, bypassing the engine entirely. Alternatively, if the brakes are the only constraint preventing movement, consider using the parking brake and driving in low gear with the clutch engaged (if manual) or holding the transmission in gear to create momentum without using fuel inefficiently for idle charging.

There is no universal RPM or duration formula because the result depends entirely on the voltage differential between your alternator's output curve and your battery's specific discharge state. For a standard 12V lead-acid system, you generally need at least 45 minutes of driving at highway speeds (where the engine is often redlined to maintain cooling) to fully recharge a deeply depleted battery while accounting for accessory loads. Idling cannot replicate this energy density transfer efficiently enough to be worth the risk of further damaging the battery chemistry or your drivetrain components.

When dealing with specific battery types, such as Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4), the requirements change drastically. These batteries have a much higher internal resistance when cold and require precise voltage windows; charging them while idling at low RPM could easily result in overcharging once the alternator regulator kicks up to 14.5V, potentially destroying the cells. Therefore, relying on engine RPM as a variable for battery health is a dangerous heuristic without real-time monitoring equipment.
